Why the cities were not appointed sooner is the first disagreement, and unusually the two sides are printed together. Calvin reads the renewed command as a reproof: that it had not occurred to their own minds to designate the cities until they were reminded indirectly censures their sluggishness, since the command had been given beyond the Jordan and the reason for it remained equally valid — so why do they wait, and why not give full effect to what they had rightly begun? He generalises: men are tardy not only to perform their duty but to provide for their own safety unless the Lord prick them forward. A note printed with his text answers him: he is somewhat singular in this, other expositors holding that the proper time had not arrived, since the appointment could not well precede the allocation of cities to the Levites, every city of refuge having to be Levitical. That is exactly Henry's view, who thinks it probable the thing was not done until the Levites had their portion assigned them in the next chapter. Henry adds that the land was newly surveyed, so they were the better able to divide its coasts into three parts for the convenient situation of the cities.

On what the law was for they agree, and Clarke supplies the mechanism. An institution of this kind was necessary wherever the patriarchal right of redemption and avenging of blood was in force, since the nearest of kin had authority to slay on the spot the man who had killed his relative; so one might casually kill another against whom he had no ill-will and lose his life to the avenger though he had not forfeited it to the law. The privileged city protected him until the cause was heard by magistrates who had authority to deliver him up if he proved not entitled to it. Calvin states the balance from the other side: the asylum gave no impunity to voluntary murder, yet respect was so far paid to the bereaved that their sorrow was not increased by the constant presence of the man who had caused it. The people were accustomed by it to detest murder, since homicide even when not culpable brought exile until the high priest's death — which showed how precious human blood is in God's sight.

Two things are pressed harder. The first is that the refuge was never meant for the murderer. Wesley notices that unwittingly is said twice, and takes the repetition to cut off all expectation wilful murderers might have of protection here, God having declared such should be taken even from his altar; from which he turns on his own age — it is strange that any Christians should make their sanctuaries protect persons whom God has so expressly excepted. The note in Calvin's text makes the same complaint, contrasting the humanity of the Mosaic appointment with the abuses of later asylums. The second is the typology, which Henry works at length: as soon as God had given them cities of rest he bade them appoint cities of refuge, which intimates what God's spiritual Israel have in Christ and heaven, not only rest to repose in but refuge to secure themselves in. So much care would not have been taken over them, he argues, when the courts could simply have been authorised to acquit the manslayer as our own law does, unless they were designed to typify the relief the gospel provides for penitent sinners. Calvin adds one observation nobody else makes, that everything here is not mentioned in order, since a man who had killed accidentally might have stayed safe by presenting himself before the court and obtaining an acquittal. Henry ends on the accident itself: the way of man is not in himself, and what reason have we to thank God who has kept us from slaying and from being slain.

The verb of appointment is read three ways. Henry notes that the original word is sanctify, and that no ceremony was used, only a public act of court declaring them sacred to the honour of God as protector of exposed innocency — if they were sanctuaries, it was proper to say they were sanctified. Calvin takes the same word toward utility rather than holiness, since it signifies also to fit, and reads it that the cities were selected as common use required, private interest yielding to public. Keil takes a different word at the next verse and rejects two renderings by name, holding it means neither cities of congregation nor cities of asylum but cities of appointment. On the placing they converge. Henry observes that the three stood so conveniently that a man might reach one in half a day from any corner, Kedesh in the most northern tribe, Hebron in the most southern, Shechem equally distant from both — God, he says, is a refuge at hand. Clarke adds that they were set on eminences to be seen at a distance, the roads to them broad and always kept in good repair; Henry makes the same point from the gospels, that a city on a hill cannot be hid, and finds comfort even in the gradient, since though the man's way at last was uphill his safety came quickly.

Why they were all Levitical draws two answers. Wesley gives two: that such causes might be more impartially examined by those best able to understand the law of God and least likely to be biassed by affection or corrupt interest, and that their reputation with the people might restrain revengeful persons who followed the manslayer thither. Henry reads it as honour and kindness at once: it made God's tribe judges in cases where divine Providence was nearly concerned, and the refugee, who might not go up to the house of the Lord, still had the servants of God's house with him to instruct him and pray for him. Calvin alone notices what the arrangement cost somebody: Kirjath-arba, afterwards Hebron, went to the Levites though it had been Caleb's property, and in that appeared the rare, nay incomparable moderation of the aged saint, who gave up city and suburbs, justly claimed as his right, the moment the lot showed this pleased God.

The names of the six cities produce the chapter's most curious agreement: two commentators give the typology and both distance themselves from it in the act. Henry says he delights not in quibbling upon names, yet is willing to notice these: Kedesh is holy, and our refuge is the holy Jesus; Shechem a shoulder, and the government is upon his shoulder; Hebron fellowship, into which believers are called; Bezer a fortification, for he is a strong-hold to them that trust in him; Ramoth exalted, for him hath God exalted; Golan joy, for in him the saints shall glory. Clarke derives the same six from their roots at greater length and hands the matter over, saying he will give each signification and leave the application to others — adding that a person of the spirit and turn of Origen could preach the whole Gospel from these particulars. Keil gives geography instead and no typology, noting that the district was called the circle of the heathen because an unusually large number of Gentiles lived there. On the last verse Clarke takes the stranger as the point: these typified the provision God was making for both Jews and Gentiles, so the stranger had the same right to it as the Israelite — is he the God of the Jews only? Henry adds a refuge the chapter does not name, the horns of the altar, which sheltered those who took hold of them where the crime was one sanctuary allowed — though a wilful murderer was to be taken even from there.
